claim: Biofilms are complex bacterial communities characterized by a high persister prevalence, which contributes to chronic and relapsing infections.
source: Biofilms are complex bacterial communities characterized by a high persister prevalence, which contributes to chronic and relapsing infections.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on biofilms and persister cells.

claim: An elevated persister frequency accompanies the stage of cell adhesion, marking the onset of biofilm development.
source: However, we observed an elevated persister frequency accompanying the stage of cell adhesion, marking the onset of biofilm development.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A comparable type of toxin-antitoxin (TA) module (TA-like system) is triggered by cell adhesion.
source: Subsequent mechanistic studies uncovered a comparable type of toxin-antitoxin (TA) module (TA-like system) triggered by cell adhesion, which is responsible for this elevation.
evidence: This claim is based on mechanistic studies described in the manuscript.

claim: The toxin HipH acts as a genotoxic deoxyribonuclease, inducing DNA double strand breaks and genome instability.
source: In this module, the toxin HipH acts as a genotoxic deoxyribonuclease, inducing DNA double strand breaks and genome instability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including in vitro DNA cleavage assays and cellular assays.

claim: The second messenger c-di-GMP functions as the antitoxin, exerting control over HipH expression and activity.
source: While the second messenger c-di-GMP functions as the antitoxin, exerting control over HipH expression and activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including pull-down assays, expression analysis, and functional assays.

claim: The dynamic interplay between c-di-GMP and HipH levels emerges as a crucial determinant governing genome stability and persister generation within biofilms.
source: The dynamic interplay between c-di-GMP and HipH levels emerges as a crucial determinant governing genome stability and persister generation within biofilms.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In biofilms, bacteria exhibit reduced antibiotic sensitivities, a phenomenon occurring independently of the presence of resistance determinants on genetic elements (Ceri et al., 1999).
source: In biofilms, bacteria exhibit reduced antibiotic sensitivities, a phenomenon occurring independently of the presence of resistance determinants on genetic elements (Ceri et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ceri et al., 1999.

claim: Antibiotic insensitivity in biofilms is linked to the elevated prevalence of persister cells in biofilms, with rates ranging from 10 to 1000 times higher compared to their planktonic counterparts (Lewis, 2005; Yan and Bassler, 2019).
source: This antibiotic insensitivity is linked to the elevated prevalence of persister cells in biofilms, with rates ranging from 10 to 1000 times higher compared to their planktonic counterparts (Lewis, 2005; Yan and Bassler, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lewis, 2005 and Yan and Bassler, 2019.

claim: Persister cells are phenotypic variants in an isogenic population that demonstrate a remarkable ability to withstand antibiotic treatment and can resuscitate once the antibiotic pressure is alleviated (Balaban et al., 2004; Bigger, 1944; Lewis, 2007; Zhou et al., 2023).
source: Persister cells, recognized as phenotypic variants in an isogenic population, demonstrate a remarkable ability to withstand antibiotic treatment and, intriguingly, can resuscitate once the antibiotic pressure is alleviated (Balaban et al., 2004; Bigger, 1944; Lewis, 2007; Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The matrix mesh size of biofilms is significantly larger than the size of molecules such as nutrients, oxygen, and antibiotics (Ganesan et al., 2016; Yan and Bassler, 2019; Yan et al., 2018).
source: Nevertheless, recent challenges to this hypothesis have arisen from studies indicating that the matrix mesh size of biofilms is significantly larger than the size of molecules such as nutrients, oxygen, and antibiotics (Ganesan et al., 2016; Yan and Bassler, 2019; Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Most antibiotics do not strongly interact with biofilm matrix components (Spoering and Lewis, 2001).
source: Notably, most antibiotics do not strongly interact with biofilm matrix components (Spoering and Lewis, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spoering and Lewis, 2001.

claim: Cells in mature biofilms exhibit metabolic activity similar to cells in the stationary phase (Nguyen et al., 2011; Walters et al., 2003; Waters et al., 2016).
source: An alternative perspective emerges from observations that cells in mature biofilms exhibit metabolic activity similar to cells in the stationary phase (Nguyen et al., 2011; Walters et al., 2003; Waters et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Elevated c-di-GMP levels function as a secondary messenger, orchestrating a shift in bacterial behavior by influencing the expression of genes crucial to biofilm development.
source: Elevated c-di-GMP levels function as a secondary messenger, orchestrating a shift in bacterial behavior by influencing the expression of genes crucial to biofilm development.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about c-di-GMP signaling in bacteria.

claim: When cells were subjected to the same duration of static culture, the persister rate within the adhered population notably surpassed that observed in the planktonic population.
source: Biphasic killing curves revealed distinct patterns. When cells were subjected to the same duration of static culture, the persister rate within the adhered population notably surpassed that observed in the planktonic population (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: The persister rate within adhered populations exhibited a positive correlation with the prolonged duration of static culture.
source: Additionally, the persister rate within adhered populations exhibited a positive correlation with the prolonged duration of static culture (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: The persister rate within planktonic populations displayed little variation with an extended duration of static culture.
source: In contrast, the persister rate within planktonic populations displayed little variation with an extended duration of static culture (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: In the initial 30 min following static incubation in microtiter dishes, the adhered subpopulation displayed a sharply peaked R–1 distribution with a low median of 0.64.
source: In the initial 30 min following static incubation in microtiter dishes, the adhered subpopulation displayed a sharply peaked R–1 distribution with a low median of 0.64 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: As the attachment duration increased to 2 hr, the R–1 distribution broadened, accompanied by a higher median of 0.93.
source: As the attachment duration increased to 2 hr, the R–1 distribution broadened, accompanied by a higher median of 0.93 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Further extension to 3.5 hr resulted in a continued broadening of the R–1 distribution, accompanied by an even higher median of 1.18.
source: Further extension to 3.5 hr resulted in a continued broadening of the R–1 distribution, accompanied by an even higher median of 1.18 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The R–1 distribution of the planktonic subpopulation from the same culture system and time points remained low, with a median of 0.31–0.35.
source: Meanwhile, the R–1 distribution of the planktonic subpopulation from the same culture system and time points remained low, with a median of 0.31–0.35, repectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Cells with the highest c-di-GMP levels were surface attached, predominantly situated at the bottom layers of the biofilm.
source: Notably, cells with the highest c-di-GMP levels were surface attached, predominantly situated at the bottom layers of the biofilm (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: This spatial distribution aligned with a subpopulation that exhibited the highest persister rate.
source: To further investigate this observation, we isolated the surface attached cells and unattached cells in the biofilms for persister counting assay. The results demonstrate that this spatial distribution aligned with a subpopulation that exhibited the highest persister rate (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Subpopulations with higher concentrations of c-di-GMP had a higher frequency of persister cells.
source: An antibiotic killing assay revealed that subpopulations with higher concentrations of c-di-GMP had a higher frequency of persister cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Cells with high intracellular c-di-GMP levels survived antibiotic treatment and resuscitated to form microcolonies.
source: Time-lapse imaging also revealed that cells with high intracellular c-di-GMP levels survived antibiotic treatment and resuscitated to form microcolonies (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Inducing PdeH expression before cell attachment disrupted cell adhesion.
source: Inducing PdeH expression before cell attachment disrupted cell adhesion, validating the efficacy of our system.
evidence: This is an experimental observation validating the PdeH overexpression system.

claim: After PdeH induction, there was a substantial decrease in c-di-GMP R–1 levels in the PdeH overexpression strain (median of 0.75) compared to the vector control strain (median of 0.98).
source: After an additional 30 min of incubation, we noted a substantial decrease in c-di-GMP R–1 levels in the PdeH overexpression strain (median of 0.75) compared to the vector control strain (median of 0.98; Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The biphasic killing curve showed significantly lower persister rates in adhered populations with PdeH overexpression compared to the vector control strain.
source: Crucially, the biphasic killing curve showed significantly lower persister rates in adhered populations with PdeH overexpression compared to the vector control strain (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After DgcZ induction, there was a substantial increase in c-di-GMP R–1 levels in the DgcZ overexpression strain (median of 1.72) compared to the vector control strain.
source: Following an additional 30 min of incubation, we noted a substantial increase in c-di-GMP R–1 levels in the DgcZ overexpression strain (median of 1.72) compared to the vector control strain (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The biphasic killing curve indicated significantly higher persister rates in adhered populations with DgcZ overexpression compared to the vector control strain.
source: Consistently, the biphasic killing curve indicated significantly higher persister rates in adhered populations with DgcZ overexpression compared to the vector control strain (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Planktonic cells with DgcZ overexpression demonstrated a significant increase in the persister ratio.
source: Consistent with the observations in adherent cells, planktonic cells with DgcZ overexpression demonstrated a significant increase in the persister ratio (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cells overexpressing DgcZ-mutant (DgcZ-m, G206A, G207A, E208Q), which lacks diguanylate cyclase activity (Boehm et al., 2009; Jonas et al., 2008), did not manifest a parallel increase in persister ratio.
source: Yet, cells overexpressing DgcZ-mutant (DgcZ-m, G206A, G207A, E208Q), which lacks diguanylate cyclase activity (Boehm et al., 2009; Jonas et al., 2008), did not manifest a parallel increase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and citations to Boehm et al., 2009 and Jonas et al., 2008.

claim: Knocking out the toxin gene hipH significantly reduces the frequency of persister formation in the presence of high levels of c-di-GMP.
source: Results show that knocking out the toxin gene hipH significantly reduces the frequency of persister formation in the presence of high levels of c-di-GMP (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The knockout of hipH alone does not lead to a significant alteration in persister frequency during the exponentially growing phase.
source: Meanwhile, the knockout of hipH alone does not lead to a significant alteration in persister frequency during the exponentially growing phase.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the screening assay.

claim: Knocking out hipA had little effect on the frequency of persister formation with elevated c-di-GMP levels.
source: In contrast, knocking out hipA had little effect on the frequency of persister formation with elevated c-di-GMP levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In in vitro biofilms, a substantial decrease in persister levels was observed following hipH knockout, contrasting with the wild-type strain that consistently displayed notably high levels of persister cells.
source: In in vitro biofilms, we observed a substantial decrease in persister levels following hipH knockout, contrasting with the wild-type strain that consistently displayed notably high levels of persister cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The wild-type UPEC16 strain displayed a notably high rate of persister formation in in vivo biofilms, while the UPEC16-ΔhipH strain exhibited a substantial reduction in persister cell frequency.
source: Consistent with the findings from in vitro biofilms, the wild-type UPEC16 strain displayed a notably high rate of persister formation. In contrast, the UPEC16-ΔhipH strain exhibited a substantial reduction in persister cell frequency under the same conditions (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A significant elevation in hipH gene expression was observed upon the overexpression of DgcZ.
source: We observed a significant elevation in hipH gene expression upon the overexpression of DgcZ (pBAD::dgcZ) (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: The strain overexpressing DgcZ-m, which is unable to increase c-di-GMP levels after induction, exhibits no activation of hipH gene expression.
source: Conversely, the strain overexpressing DgcZ-m, which is unable to increase c-di-GMP levels after induction, exhibit no activation of hipH gene expression (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Fluorescent imaging revealed a positive correlation between HipH and c-di-GMP expression at the single-cell level, supported by a correlation coefficient of 0.694.
source: Fluorescent imaging revealed a positive correlation between HipH and c-di-GMP expression at the single-cell level (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), supported by a correlation coefficient of 0.694 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: HipH overexpression substantially inhibits cell growth, with only 9.8 ± 3.4% of cells retaining growth potential.
source: The results demonstrated that HipH overexpression substantially inhibit cell growth, with only 9.8 ± 3.4% of cells retaining growth potential (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Growth-inhibited cells from HipH overexpression revealed a predominant presence of Viable but Non-Culturable (VBNC) cells (Ayrapetyan et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2023; Pan and Ren, 2022), constituting 72 ± 5% of the total cell population, alongside a significant proportion of dead cells, accounting for 17.9 ± 2.3% of the total cells.
source: Further analysis of the growth-inhibited cells revealed a predominant presence of Viable but Non-Culturable (VBNC) cells (Ayrapetyan et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2023; Pan and Ren, 2022), constituting 72 ± 5% of the total cell population, alongside a significant proportion of dead cells, accounting for 17.9 ± 2.3% of the total cells (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J and citations to relevant literature.

claim: Strains co-overexpressing HipH and c-di-GMP exhibited significantly recovered growth potential compared to the strain overexpressing HipH alone.
source: Comparing to the strain overexpressing HipH alone, those strains co-overexpressing HipH and c-di-GMP exhibited a significantly recovered growth potential (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: 36 ± 6.7% of cells retained growth potential in the strain expressing HipH and DosC, while approximately 85 ± 18% retained growth potential in the strain expressing HipH and DgcZ.
source: Specifically, 36 ± 6.7% of cells retained growth potential in the strain expressing HipH and DosC, while approximately 85 ± 18% retained growth potential in the strain expressing HipH and DgcZ.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the growth potential assay.

claim: The truncated mutant of HipH, lacking the kinase catalytic motif (Δ5, amino acid 340–372), demonstrated a comparable ability to inhibit cell growth and induced VBNCs compared to the intact HipH.
source: The truncated mutant of HipH, lacking the kinase catalytic motif (Δ5, amino acid 340–372), demonstrated a comparable ability to inhibit cell growth and induced VBNCs compared to the intact HipH (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Overexpression of mutants lacking the DNA binding domain HTH (Δ1 and Δ2) did not inhibit cell growth or induce VBNCs or dead cells.
source: Our results showed that overexpression of mutants lacking the DNA binding domain HTH (Δ1 and Δ2) did not inhibit cell growth or induce VBNCs or dead cells (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Fluorescent microscopy confirmed the nucleoid localization of wild-type HipH.
source: Consistent with these results, fluorescent microscopy confirmed the nucleoid localization of wild-type HipH (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescent microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: qPCR analysis revealed a significant upregulation of SOS response genes, such as recA, sulA, and tisB, in cells overexpressing HipH.
source: qPCR analysis revealed a significant upregulation of SOS response genes, such as recA, sulA, and tisB, in cells overexpressing HipH (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The near abolition of cell growth potential upon knockout of recA in cells overexpressing HipH supports the conclusion that HipH induces DNA damage.
source: Notably, the near abolition of cell growth potential upon knockout of recA, a crucial protein essential for DNA damage repair, in cells overexpressing HipH further supports the conclusion that HipH induces DNA damage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HipH has the capability to cleave supercoiled plasmids, leading to the production of double-strand breaks (DSBs), as evidenced by prominent smears observed on agarose gels.
source: The results demonstrated HipH's capability to cleave supercoiled plasmids, leading to the production of double-strand breaks (DSBs), as evidenced by prominent smears observed on agarose gels (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro DNA cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: There is a positive correlation between HipH's DNA cleavage capacity and its protein concentration, temperature, and incubation time.
source: Further analysis revealed a positive correlation between HipH's DNA cleavage capacity and its protein concentration, temperature, and incubation time (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: The overexpression of RecG successfully rescued growth-deficient cells resulting from HipH overexpression.
source: The overexpression of RecG, a key player in the repair of DSBs in DNA (Whitby et al., 1994), successfully rescued growth-deficient cells resulting from HipH overexpression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and a citation to Whitby et al., 1994.

claim: A biotinylated c-di-GMP pull-down assay (Figure 5A; Chambers and Sauer, 2017), conducted from both cell lysate and purified protein, revealed a physical binding between c-di-GMP and HipH.
source: A biotinylated c-di-GMP pull-down assay (Figure 5A; Chambers and Sauer, 2017), conducted from both cell lysate and purified protein, revealed a physical binding between c-di-GMP and HipH (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5A-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B, and a citation to Chambers and Sauer, 2017.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) between c-di-GMP and HipH was determined as 7.6 μM.
source: The dissociation constant (KD), calculated based on the concentration of c-di-GMP at which half-maximal binding of HipH occurs, was determined as 7.6 μM (Figure 5B, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: c-di-GMP successfully displaced HipH-GFP-His from HipH-GFP-His/biotin-c-di-GMP complexes, while other nucleotides such as cAMP and GTP did not exhibit the same effect.
source: Additionally, c-di-GMP successfully displaced HipH-GFP-His from HipH-GFP-His/biotin-c-di-GMP complexes, while other nucleotides such as cAMP and GTP did not exhibit the same effect (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The addition of c-di-GMP exerted a significant suppressive effect on the cleavage activity of HipH for both relaxed and supercoiled plasmids, as evidenced by a reduction of smears and double-strand break (DSB) bands on agarose gels.
source: Subsequently, we introduced c-di-GMP into the HipH DNA-cleavage assay system, and notably, its addition exerted a significant suppressive effect on the cleavage activity of HipH. This effect was observed for both relaxed and supercoiled plasmids, as evidenced by a reduction of smears and double-strand break (DSB) bands on agarose gels (Figure 5F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro DNA cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5F-I.

claim: Other nucleotides, including cAMP and GTP, did not demonstrate the same suppressive effect on HipH's cleavage activity.
source: It is noteworthy that other nucleotides, including cAMP and GTP, did not demonstrate the same suppressive effect on HipH's cleavage activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HipB failed to inhibit HipH's DNase activity.
source: However, when we tested the potential impact of HipB on HipH's DNase activity by purifying and introducing HipB into our cleavage system, we found that HipB failed to inhibit HipH's DNase activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cells overexpressing HipH alone displayed Gam-GFP foci in 8.85 ± 1.28% of cases, while only 0.30 ± 0.12% of wild-type cells demonstrated such foci.
source: Microscopic examination revealed that cells overexpressing HipH alone displayed Gam-GFP foci in 8.85 ± 1.28% of cases, while only 0.30 ± 0.12% of wild-type cells demonstrated such foci (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: Elevation of intracellular c-di-GMP levels resulted in a significant reduction in the percentage of cells with Gam-GFP foci, with DosC addition decreasing the occurrence to 1.34 ± 0.39% and DgcZ to 0.46 ± 0.19%.
source: Further investigations showed that elevation of intracellular c-di-GMP levels resulted in a significant reduction in the percentage of cells with Gam-GFP foci, with DosC addition decreasing the occurrence to 1.34 ± 0.39% and DgcZ to 0.46 ± 0.19% (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: Cell adhesion, a pivotal event initiating biofilm development, emerges as a trigger for persister formation.
source: Our investigation reveals that cell adhesion, a pivotal event initiating biofilm development, emerges as a trigger for persister formation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: UPEC is the predominant cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and responsible for approximately 80% of cases.
source: To enhance the clinical relevance of our study, we employed UPEC, the predominant cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and responsible for approximately 80% of cases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about UPEC.

claim: UPEC has a notable ability to form biofilms on various surfaces, including catheter materials, bladder epithelial cell walls, and within bladder cells.
source: UPEC has a notable ability to form biofilms on various surfaces, including catheter materials, bladder epithelial cell walls, and within bladder cells (Supplementary Information).
evidence: This is established knowledge about UPEC biofilm formation.

claim: UPEC16 demonstrates a significant phylogenetic similarity to established UPEC reference strains such as CFT073 and UTI89.
source: This strain demonstrates a significant phylogenetic similarity to established UPEC reference strains such as CFT073 and UTI89 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The increase in c-di-GMP levels is a distinctive feature of cell-surface adhesion, marking the transition of cells from a planktonic lifestyle to a sessile one (Fernandez et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2015; Valentini and Filloux, 2016).
source: The increase in c-di-GMP levels is a distinctive feature of cell-surface adhesion, marking the transition of cells from a planktonic lifestyle to a sessile one (Fernandez et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2015; Valentini and Filloux, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Guanosine pentaphosphate and tetraphosphate ((p)ppGpp), key alarmones in the bacterial stringent response, have been shown to mediate ribosome dimerization, leading to persistence, while their degradation triggers resuscitation (Song and Wood, 2020; Wood and Song, 2020; Wood et al., 2019).
source: Guanosine pentaphosphate and tetraphosphate ((p)ppGpp), key alarmones in the bacterial stringent response, have been shown to mediate ribosome dimerization, leading to persistence, while their degradation triggers resuscitation. This dual function of (p)ppGpp underscores its significance in both initiating and terminating the persister state (Song and Wood, 2020; Wood and Song, 2020; Wood et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature on (p)ppGpp.

claim: The interaction between cyclic AMP (cAMP) and the cAMP receptor protein (CRP) has been identified as a crucial regulator of bacterial persistence (Mok et al., 2015; Niu et al., 2024).
source: Additionally, the interaction between cyclic AMP (cAMP) and the cAMP receptor protein (CRP) has been identified as a crucial regulator of bacterial persistence. The cAMP-CRP complex acts as a global regulator, influencing persistence through modulation of cellular metabolism and regulation of stress responses (Mok et al., 2015; Niu et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on cAMP-CRP regulation.

claim: HipH has been identified as a Ser/Thr protein kinase involved in regulating ribosome assembly and cell metabolism.
source: Previous studies believed it a homolog of the toxin protein HipA, functioning as a Ser/Thr protein kinase involved in regulating ribosome assembly and cell metabolism (Gratani et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gratani et al., 2023.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated HipH's primary protein substrates to be the ribosomal protein RpmE (L31) and the carbon storage regulator CsrA (Gratani et al., 2023).
source: Previous studies have identified HipH as a Ser/Thr protein kinase, sharing homology with the well-characterized toxin HipA. These studies demonstrated its primary protein substrates to be the ribosomal protein RpmE (L31) and the carbon storage regulator CsrA (Gratani et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gratani et al., 2023.

claim: It has been reported that HipB serves as an antitoxin for HipH (Gratani et al., 2023; Maeda et al., 2017).
source: Furthermore, it has been reported that HipB serves as an antitoxin for HipH (Gratani et al., 2023; Maeda et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gratani et al., 2023 and Maeda et al., 2017.

claim: Targeting the c-di-GMP-HipH toxin-antitoxin system effectively inhibited drug tolerance in Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) infections.
source: Notably, targeting this toxin-antitoxin system effectively inhibited drug tolerance in Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) infections, presenting promising therapeutic strategies against chronic and relapsing infections.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the therapeutic implications of the findings.
